analysis.one_liner: Funds state and nonprofit pilots giving gig and freelance workers benefits they can carry between jobs.
analysis.headline: This bipartisan bill — sponsored by one Democrat and five cosponsors from three parties — was referred to the Senate labor committee in May 2023 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a small federal pilot program run by the Department of Labor. It would give $20 million in competitive grants to states, local governments, and nonprofits to design, test, and evaluate ways to provide benefits — health coverage, disability protection, paid leave, skills training, and savings — to independent contractors, freelancers, temp workers, and other workers who fall outside traditional full-time employment. The point of 'portable' benefits is that a worker keeps them when moving from job to job, unlike benefits tied to a single employer. A government watchdog would then report to Congress on what the pilots achieved.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent workers — rideshare and delivery drivers, freelancers, contract and temp workers — who currently get little or no benefits like workers' compensation, disability coverage, or paid leave, since those benefits normally come attached to a single full-time employer. States, local governments, and nonprofits would receive grant money to build and test benefit models, and workers in those pilot programs would be the first to gain actual benefits if the pilots work.

how_it_helps.text: Creates competitive Department of Labor grants for FY2023 to states, local governments, and nonprofits to design, implement, and evaluate portable benefit models for independent workers [S2] [S3].

Requires grant-funded models to cover benefits commonly provided to full-time employees — workers' compensation, skills training, disability coverage, health insurance, retirement saving, income security, and short-term saving — and bars funding for retirement-only models [S3].
Directs the Comptroller General to evaluate the grants and report to Congress by September 30, 2025, including their impact on workers' compensation [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through a $20 million authorization for fiscal year 2023 ($5 million for improving existing models, $15 million for new ones). Any lasting change — such as requiring companies that hire independent workers to contribute — would come only from future legislation built on what the pilots find.

drawbacks.text: The program is small and experimental: $20 million funds pilot designs and studies, not benefits for most workers, and no independent worker is guaranteed anything unless a future Congress acts on the results [S3].

A good-faith objection: building a benefits system around 'independent contractor' status could entrench that classification, leaving workers with thinner benefits than employees get, instead of pushing companies to reclassify them as employees with full legal protections.

Grants go to states and nonprofits rather than directly to workers, so results depend on which models are chosen and whether they can be scaled nationally — a standard the Secretary must consider but cannot guarantee [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is small and the idea is aimed at a real and growing gap: workers outside traditional employment generally lack benefits entirely. But the bill is a modest first step — it funds experiments and evaluations, not benefits for workers today — and a pilot alone settles nothing about whether portable benefits or full employee reclassification is the better fix. The honest weighing: low cost, genuine long-term potential, no immediate benefit to workers unless follow-up legislation follows.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 2023 and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Mark Warner (D-VA) introduced the bill on May 18, 2023, joined by five cosponsors: Republicans Young, Cramer, and Hoeven, Independent King, and Democrat Bennet [S3] [S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
That was the last action of record: the committee held no markup, the Senate never voted, and no companion measure advanced in the House during the 118th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that rely on independent contractors and pay them no benefits are no closer to being asked to contribute to portable benefit systems, because the pilot program that could have built and tested those models never got a committee vote. Independent workers remain where they were, with no benefits attached to their work.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firms using contractor labor; nothing changed

for.name: Sen. Mark Warner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it, proposing a Labor Department pilot grant program for portable benefits

for.name: Sens. Todd Young, Kevin Cramer, John Hoeven, Angus King, and Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it support from three Republicans, one Independent, and one Democrat

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in May 2023 and never scheduled a markup or advanced it during the 118th Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill had cosponsors from three parties at introduction — three of 49 Senate Republicans, the one Independent sponsor-aligned member, and one of 48 Senate Democrats alongside lead sponsor Warner [S4] — and it died without any vote, so no party ever had to vote against it.

industries.industry: Gig platforms and companies that hire independent contractors
industries.note: The pilot itself costs these companies nothing, but it is a step toward models where they would contribute to workers' benefits, which is why portable benefit proposals are closely watched by rideshare, delivery, and staffing firms. Workers at these companies are the intended beneficiaries, so the industry's interest and workers' interest pull apart only if and when a funding mandate follows the pilots.

industries.industry: States, local governments, and nonprofit organizations
industries.note: They would receive the $20 million in grants to design and run portable benefit pilots, and workers in their programs would be the first to see benefits.
